summary.short: Requires persons who use training datasets of registered copyrighted works to train or release generative AI models to file a notice with the Register of Copyrights 30 days before commercial use or release. Copyright owners may sue for civil penalties.
summary.long: The bill, titled the CLEAR Act, requires any person that uses a training dataset in connection with training or release of a generative AI model to submit to the Register of Copyrights a notice containing a sufficiently detailed summary of each copyrighted work in the dataset, and the dataset's URL if it is publicly available. For models first used or released on or after the effective date, notice is due 30 days before commercial use (including internal use) or release; for earlier models, notice is due 30 days after the Register issues implementing regulations, which must be issued within 180 days of the effective date. A copyright owner may sue in a United States district court for failure to file; the court may impose a civil penalty of at least $5,000 per instance, capped at $2,500,000 in total per person per year, may enjoin use until notice is submitted, and may award attorney's fees. The Register must maintain a publicly available online database of notices. The Act takes effect 180 days after enactment.

relations.note: The definition of 'copyrighted work' refers to title 17 for protection, and to sections 408 and 1401 of title 17 for registration and scheduling. The bill does not otherwise cite title 17.

evidence.quote: protected under title 17, United States Code

notes: Text as introduced; the document gives no version date. Sec. 2(b)(2)(A) and (B) use different filing triggers. Sec. 2(b)(2)(B) runs from Register regulations, which Sec. 2(b)(3) requires within 180 days after the effective date, and Sec. 2(e) sets the effective date at 180 days after enactment, so the (B) deadline has no fixed date in the text. Because 'copyrighted work' requires registration or scheduling (Sec. 2(a)(2)), the notice duty and the cause of action in Sec. 2(c)(1) reach only registered or scheduled works. thresholds.note: No numeric cutoff in the text changes scope, eligibility, exemption, obligation tier or prohibition. The dollar figures ($5,000 minimum per instance in Sec. 2(c)(2)(A)(i) and the $2,500,000 annual limit in Sec. 2(c)(3)(A)) are penalty amounts and are recorded under enforcement, not thresholds. The day counts (Sec. 2(b)(2), (b)(3), (e)) are procedural time limits and deadlines, recorded as events. The definitions in Sec. 2(a) contain no numeric cutoff.
